rights: Working copies from a paid Newspapers.com session for research. Canonical share link is the newspapers.com image URL. Do not put full page scans on the public site until each item has a short excerpt crop, a citation, and a clip share URL from Newspapers.com.

embedPlan.now: Link the newspapers.com image URL. Keep the local PNG as a preview.
embedPlan.next: On each keeper page, use Clip to create a Newspapers.com clip. That gives a /clip/ID/ URL that can be shared and later embedded.

clips.quote: Colored Newspaper Burned Out. The Echo, a weekly negro newspaper published at Long Branch, was burned out recently. The fire which is thought to be of incendiary origin damaged the machinery and press-room of the newspaper to the extent of several hundred dollars. The first issue of the paper was edited by Rock & Howard.
clips.why: Founding-year confirmation, editors, suspected arson, Long Branch plant

clips.quote: ECHO MOVES TO RED BANK. The Echo edited and published in the interest of the colored race in Long Branch by W. E. Rock for the past five years, has moved to Red Bank, where Editor Rock has purchased a home.
clips.why: Exact move date and five-year Long Branch run. URL may need the live image id from oldest-nj.json if this one 404s.

clips.quote: R. HENRI HERBERT'S ATTACK. He Asks His Colored Fellow-Citizens to Help Defeat Founder Bradley.
clips.why: Herbert, after the Sentinel years, organizing against Asbury Park pavilion segregation. Same fight as Murrell that summer.

clips.quote: R. HENRI HERBERT NOT LEFT. Appointed as a Consulting Member of the Republican State Committee.
clips.why: Post-Sentinel political standing of the founder

clips.quote: Colonel Murrell, editor of the New Jersey Trumpet, later James A. Bradley entered and was greeted with applause. The meeting was called to discuss the signs which James A. Bradley had posted on the pavilions forbidding their occupancy to the colored race.
clips.why: NJ daily treats the Trumpet editor as a public actor in a segregation fight

clips.quote: Colonel Murrell, editor of the New Jersey Trumpet, was then introduced as the speaker of the evening.
clips.why: Same Asbury Park meeting, front page

clips.quote: The New Jersey Afro-American — published in Newark — was one of a chain of Black-owned and edited papers... the New Jersey edition no longer exists.
clips.why: NJ paper prints a 1947 masthead photo and states the edition is gone

clips.quote: Alfred P. Smith served as The Landscape's editor, reporter, publisher, printer, translator, circulation and advertising managers. Originally distributed under the banner of A.P. Smith's Paper... from May of 1881 until July of 1901.
clips.why: Tom Brady on Alfred P. Smith: The Landscape, first as A.P. Smith's Paper, printed at East Allendale Road from May 1881 until July 1901.

clips.quote: In 1881, Smith, a former reporter who owned a job-printing business, started a monthly newspaper first called "A. P. Smith's Paper" and then renamed "The Landscape." Most of Smith's subscribers were white.
clips.why: Second Look: Writer shaped civil-rights Landscape. Alfred P. Smith started A. P. Smith's Paper in 1881, then renamed it The Landscape.

clips.quote: By himself and out of an old house overlooking the Saddle River valley, Alfred P. Smith edited and printed what was purportedly the nation's smallest newspaper. Its four pages of newsprint paper measured 6 x 8 inches.
clips.why: Nancy R. Peck: Alfred P. Smith printed what was called the nation's smallest newspaper from an old house overlooking the Saddle River valley.

clips.quote: in an article just published in The New Jersey Guardian, a journal for colored readers which has state-wide circulation.
clips.why: Paterson News cites The New Jersey Guardian as a journal for colored readers with state-wide circulation.

clips.quote: Another prospective commission candidate is Melvin B. Johnson of 55 Somerset st., former Negro newspaper publisher and editor. Johnson was in the newspaper field until 1946, when he left to work among Negro voters in Gov. Driscoll's gubernatorial campaign.
clips.why: Melvin B. Johnson named as former Negro newspaper publisher and editor, in the field until 1946.
